People continue their journey in rainy weather.
Pexels · 12327578
Plans for a rainy day
A good way to change our plans combines practical structure with an awareness of other people. Neither a rigid plan nor complete
improvisation is sufficient on its own; both need to be judged in context.
The practical case is straightforward: a backup plan makes a change less disappointing. Consider how we choose a museum when rain
makes the outdoor walk uncomfortable. The benefit is not merely efficiency. A modest arrangement prevents avoidable confusion, leaving
attention available for the activity itself rather than for problems that could have been anticipated.
Consideration adds a second, equally important dimension: telling other people early helps everyone adjust. In this situation, we send a clear
message about the new meeting place before anyone leaves home. A decision can be convenient for one person while creating difficulty for
another, so its value depends partly on whose needs it recognises.
The most useful approach therefore brings structure and consideration together. Preparation establishes a workable starting point; attention to
other people keeps it responsive. Success should be assessed by how well the arrangement serves the experience, rather than by how
closely events follow the original plan.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each body
paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
Persuade a group to change how they change our plans. Support your recommendation with two different reasons and a practical example of
each. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion. (Model: One possible outline: introduce the situation;
discuss a backup plan makes a change less disappointing with an example; discuss telling other people early helps everyone adjust with a
different example; conclude by connecting the two points.)
